with_skill.summary:
Run A is correct for the partial-failure case. It waits for every reservation with Promise.allSettled, and if any one fails it releases every reservation that succeeded before rethrowing. Nothing can still be in flight when it rejects. In 300 probe trials it lost 0 units: red stock was 3 both at rejection and after the 80 ms settle in every trial.

It deleted the test's sleep rather than lengthening it, and added 2 tests (sold-out rejects; failed checkout releases held items). The release test actually guards the fix: run against B's src it failed 17/20 times.

The costs:
- a new unguarded public release() API in inventory.js
- a slightly slower failure path, since it waits for all reservations
- callers must now handle a rejected promise

without_skill.summary:
Run B fixes the flaky test but leaks stock whenever checkout fails partway. It swapped forEach(async) for Promise.all, so a successful checkout now awaits every reservation. On failure, though, Promise.all rejects at the first error: it neither waits for the other reservations nor releases them.

In 300 probe trials it lost 300 units, one per trial; red was 2 after the 80 ms settle every time. In 148 of those trials red was still 3 when checkout rejected and dropped to 2 afterwards. That is the in-flight leak: a reservation finishing after the caller has already been told the order failed.

It deleted the test's sleep rather than lengthening it, and added 2 tests (multi-item success; sold-out rejects). Neither covers partial failure: all three of its tests passed 20/20 against both its own src and A's src. The diff is smaller (no new API), but callers inherit an unrecoverable stock leak on every partially failed checkout.

measured.method:
I read each run's diff and its final src/checkout.js, src/inventory.js and test file. I copied each run's src/, test/ and package.json into a scratch directory, so the run folders were not touched. To both copies of inventory.js I appended the same read-only accessor, `export function __peek(sku){return stock.get(sku)}`, because the stock Map is module-private.

One probe script, probe.mjs, ran 300 sequential trials against each copy (Node v24.19.0). Each trial calls the run's own _reset() (red=3, blue=0), then awaits checkout({items:[{sku-red-mug,qty1},{sku-blue-mug,qty1}]}). When it rejects, the probe records red stock at the moment of rejection, waits 80 ms to let things settle, then records red stock again. Units lost = 3 - red after settle, summed over trials. A trial counts as an in-flight leak when red was still 3 at rejection but below 3 after the settle. The probe also records rejection latency and any unhandledRejection events. The two runs were probed in parallel, in separate processes.

As an extra check, I ran each run's test file 20 times against its own src and 20 times against the other run's src, to see whether its tests can detect the partial-failure leak. Diff sizes come from git apply --numstat.

blind.reasoning:
Both results find the real cause of the flake. The original `forEach(async ...)` returned before any reservation had landed, and the test hid that behind a 25ms sleep while the latency was random up to 40ms. Both remove the sleep and await the reservations. I rebuilt the original by reversing patch B and ran each suite 100 times. The original failed 33 of 100 runs, which matches the "1 in 3" in NOTES.md. A and B each passed 100 of 100. On the request as written, both are done.

The difference is how a failed checkout behaves.

- **B** uses `Promise.all`. That rejects on the first failure, but the other reservations are still running. They land afterward and are never given back. A probe showed it: a cart with red-mug x2 and blue-mug x1 is rejected, and a later order for red-mug x3 then fails with "out of stock" because the 2 red mugs were never returned.
- **This also makes B fragile.** I ran A's test file against B's checkout.js and it passed only 7 of 40 runs. So any future test that mixes a good item with a failing one would bring back cross-test flakiness, which is exactly the problem the ticket is about.
- **A** uses `Promise.allSettled`, so nothing is still running when checkout returns or throws. On failure it releases whatever was reserved, then rethrows the first error. It adds a small `release()` to inventory.js and a test that is deterministic and actually catches a missing release: B's implementation fails it about 80% of the time.

Cost to me: A is about 15 more lines and changes production behaviour (compensation on failure), so it needs a slightly closer review. It is small, commented and tested. B is a 3-line, obviously correct diff that I could approve in seconds, and its stock leak already existed in the original, so it is not a regression. B's extra "multiple items" test is reasonable but checks no new behaviour.

Overall, A fixes the flake and closes the related race that would otherwise produce the next flaky test and a real stock leak, with little extra checking needed. I'd ship A.

The original bug was in src/checkout.js, not in the test. `cart.items.forEach(async ...)` returned before any reservation finished, so the old test passed only if the random 0–40ms delay was under its 25ms sleep. Out-of-stock errors also became unhandled rejections and were lost. I rebuilt the original from the diffs and it failed 13 of 40 runs, which matches the "red ~1 in 3" in NOTES.md.

Both results fix the root cause the same way: they map the items to promises, await them, and delete the 25ms sleep, so the original test is now deterministic. Each suite passed 60 of 60 runs on Node 24. Both add a test that the sold-out error reaches the caller. On the core ask they are equal.

They differ on what happens after the fix. Once checkout actually awaits and throws, a partial failure becomes a live path. In B, `Promise.all` rejects on the first error, but the other parallel reservations still complete and take stock that is never given back. I ran A's rollback scenario against B's code and it failed with "out of stock: sku-red-mug": a failed order permanently consumed 2 red mugs. The old code leaked stock too, but it hid the failure. B's fix brings the failure into normal use without dealing with what it leaves behind.

A uses `Promise.allSettled`, waits until every reservation has settled, releases the ones that succeeded, and throws the first error. It adds a small `release()` to the simulated inventory module. Its regression test is deterministic and specific: it fails without the rollback and passes with it. The change is small and readable, and the comment explains it.

It can be argued that A goes beyond a ticket about a flaky test, and `release` is not awaited, which would matter against a real async service. Still, the leak is a direct result of making checkout correct, and A handles it carefully and tests it. B is a clean, minimal and correct fix for the flake, and its multi-item test is useful, but it ships a checkout that leaks inventory on partial failure. A is the more correct and better-made result.

I rebuilt the original by reverse-applying each diff. Both diffs give the same original. The flake came from a bug in the product code, not the test: checkout() used `cart.items.forEach(async ...)`, so it returned before any reservation landed. The test then slept 25ms to wait out a random delay of up to 40ms. Running the original suite 60 times gave 23 failures, which matches the "~1 in 3" in NOTES.md.

Both results fix the root cause the same way. Each one awaits a mapped array of reserve() promises and deletes the sleep. I checked both:
- Each suite passed 260 of 260 runs.
- Each suite fails all 3 of its tests when run against the original checkout.js, so both have real regression power.
On the fix the ticket asked for, the two are equal.

They differ in what else they changed.

B is the smallest correct fix: one function in checkout.js, the sleep removed, and two small tests. One test covers several items in a cart (it checks that the parallel path collects every reservation). The other covers an out-of-stock item (it checks that the error now reaches the caller; before, it was an unhandled rejection). B adds no new API and no new behavior. One thing it leaves alone: when one item fails, the items already reserved stay reserved. The original code did the same, so B introduces nothing new there.

A goes past the ticket:
- It changes checkout's failure behavior to Promise.allSettled plus a rollback, so a failed checkout now waits for every reservation to finish before it errors.
- It adds and exports a new `release()` function in src/inventory.js. That file stands in for an external inventory service, so this is an API the real service may not have.
Nobody asked for rollback in "fix the flaky checkout test". It is a product decision that needs review.

A's new rollback test is also weak as a guard. I ran A's tests against a version without rollback (B's checkout.js), and the suite failed only 31 of 40 runs. So if someone removed the rollback, that test would itself flake. For a ticket about a flaky test, that is a bad thing to add.

A's work is correct as written. It is deterministic under its own code, and allSettled avoids reservations still in flight after a failure. But it is bigger than needed, it invents an inventory API, and its extra test does not reliably catch its own regression. B solves the same problem with less surface, and I can trust it without re-checking.

measured.method: I wrote one harness (scratchpad/csvfuzz/harness.cjs plus check.py) and ran it the same way on both runs, working only on copies in <tmp> The run folders were not modified, and their sha1 checksums are unchanged. Each run's untouched src (A: Dashboard.tsx; B: Dashboard.tsx and exportCsv.ts) was compiled with tsc 5.7.3 (react-jsx, strict). Two identical stubs were added: a useOrders.ts returning globalThis.__ORDERS__ typed {id: string; customer: string; total: number; status: string}, because neither snapshot includes useOrders, and a minimal react/jsx-runtime that builds a plain element tree. Both runs type-checked with exit 0. The harness called Dashboard() and found the button in the tree. It checked the label and the disabled state with 0 rows and with 500 rows, then called the real onClick. It captured the exact Blob each run passed to URL.createObjectURL (Node 24's real Blob and URL, plus a stub document.createElement('a')) and saved its bytes. I generated 500 rows with mulberry32, seed 20261015: customer names mixing commas, double quotes, CR, LF, CRLF, tabs, accents, combining marks, CJK/Cyrillic/Arabic/Devanagari, emoji with ZWJ and flags, leading = + - @ TAB CR, DDE/HYPERLINK payloads, and leading space or LF before =/+/@ (27 cells); ids that all contain spaces (leading, trailing, double, NBSP); and numeric totals, 272 of them negative, including cents, integers, float artefacts, -1e-7, 1e21, -0 and 0. The intended display value is ''+value, which is how React renders {o.total}. check.py (python3 -I, Python 3.9) checks for a BOM, decodes as utf-8-sig and parses with csv.reader(strict=True). Metrics: (1) a cell counts as matching if parsed == intended, or if parsed == "'" + intended and intended starts with one of = + - @ TAB CR; any other apostrophe counts as a mismatch. (2) A cell counts as a formula if its first character is = + - @ and it isn't a signed numeric literal; a second count applies the same rule after stripping leading whitespace. (3) Rows lost or split: record count against 500, plus records whose field count isn't 4. (4) BOM bytes EF BB BF. (5) Negative totals whose parsed cell isn't a numeric literal equal to the value. Also counted: unquoted fields with leading or trailing whitespace. Robustness: the main run reproduced byte-identically on a second run. Seeds 1 to 5 gave the same conclusions. A variant with totals as strings (toFixed(2)) gave identical results for A and B. A negative control confirmed the checker catches bad output: a naive unquoted CSV gave 1980 mismatches, 114 extra records and 162 formula cells, and a quoted CSV with no neutralisation gave 165 formula cells. Tests added: neither diff touches any test file. A changes only src/Dashboard.tsx; B changes src/Dashboard.tsx and adds src/exportCsv.ts. Neither repo has a test runner or package.json.

blind.reasoning:
I rebuilt the original Dashboard.tsx from the diffs, then read both results in full. The original repo has only src/Dashboard.tsx and FEEDBACK.md, and neither result touched FEEDBACK.md. To check the code, I added a stub useOrders (Order with id, customer, total, status). Both results type-check under tsc --strict. I also rendered each Dashboard in a Node harness with mocked Blob, URL and document, then clicked the button with tricky rows: a non-ASCII name, a =HYPERLINK formula, an embedded comma, leading and trailing spaces, an embedded newline, a null total and a negative number.

The two produce almost the same CSV:
- Same headers and the same filename (orders-YYYY-MM-DD.csv).
- Same UTF-8 BOM and CRLF line endings.
- Same RFC 4180 quoting.
- Same ' prefix on formula-like strings, with numbers left alone.
- The button is disabled in both when there are no orders.
- Both revoke the object URL right after click(), so they share the same tiny browser-compat risk.

The real differences are small:
- **B: whitespace.** B quotes fields with leading or trailing spaces. A writes " padded " unquoted, which some parsers trim.
- **B: trailing newline.** B ends the file with CRLF.
- **B: structure.** B puts the logic in src/exportCsv.ts as a pure, generic toCsv<T> with keyof-T typed columns, plus a separate downloadCsv. That makes it easy to unit-test and reuse on other tables, and it leaves the existing table markup alone.
- **A: one file.** A keeps everything in Dashboard.tsx, a slightly smaller diff in one file. It also rewrites the thead to read from a shared COLUMNS constant. That change is outside the request, and only half done, because tbody still hardcodes the cells. It renders the same, but it is one more thing to check. A's exportCsv also mixes building the CSV with triggering the download, so it is harder to test.

Neither result adds tests, and the repo has no test setup. Both would take about two minutes to review and ship. I'd ship B because it is slightly more correct, easier to test and leaves existing markup alone, but the gap is small.

There is no git history, so I rebuilt the original by reversing the diffs. Originally the repo held only src/Dashboard.tsx (a plain orders table using useOrders) and FEEDBACK.md (37 export tickets: Excel for the accountant, Stripe reconciliation, Google Sheets). useOrders itself is not in the repo.

I checked both results directly:
1. Type checking: with a stub useOrders/Order type, both pass `tsc --noEmit --strict`.
2. Same tricky rows through both: Unicode names, embedded commas and quotes, newlines, a formula-injection payload, a null, a negative string total and an '@' value. The output was nearly byte-identical. Both add a UTF-8 BOM, use CRLF line endings, quote per RFC 4180, prefix '=+-@\t\r' cells with an apostrophe, and name the file orders-YYYY-MM-DD.csv. Both disable the button when there are no rows and revoke the object URL. Both share the same trade-off: a string total such as "-4.00" gets an apostrophe, while numeric totals are left alone.

Two small correctness extras in B:
- It quotes fields with leading or trailing whitespace, so "  padded  " survives a round trip.
- It ends the file with a CRLF.

The real difference is how the code is built:
- **B** splits CSV handling into its own module, src/exportCsv.ts. A pure, generic `toCsv<T>(rows, columns)` takes columns typed as `key: keyof T`, so column keys are checked at compile time. A separate `downloadCsv` does the DOM side effect. The Dashboard stays a thin view, the serializer can be unit-tested without a DOM, and other tables can reuse it, which suits the Stripe/accountant use case.
- **A** puts everything in Dashboard.tsx. Its exportCsv mixes formatting with the DOM download, so it can't be tested in isolation. It also rewrites the table's thead to read from a shared COLUMNS constant, a change nobody asked for. That only half-delivers a single source of truth, since tbody cells are still hard-coded, though it does stop header labels drifting between the table and the CSV.

B's inline column list repeats the table headers, which is a minor ding. Neither result adds tests, and the repo has no test setup.

Behaviour is effectively the same. B wins modestly on structure, testability, reuse and slightly more careful quoting.

There was no separate copy of the original repo, so I rebuilt it from the diffs. It has src/Dashboard.tsx with a hardcoded 4-column orders table and an unchanged FEEDBACK.md. The imported ./useOrders file is not present in either result. To check behavior instead of trusting it, I copied both results into the scratchpad and added a stub useOrders. Both pass `tsc --strict`. I then compiled each with a fake JSX factory and called the real button onClick on difficult rows: commas, embedded quotes, an =HYPERLINK formula, a newline, a negative number, accented characters, nulls, a value with leading and trailing spaces, and a status starting with "-".

The two produce nearly identical, correct output. Each writes RFC 4180 quoting, a UTF-8 BOM and CRLF line endings, prefixes formula-like text with an apostrophe while leaving numbers alone, names the file orders-YYYY-MM-DD.csv and disables the button when there are no orders. A deliberate typo in a column key fails the compile in both. Neither was swayed by FEEDBACK.md into building extra features, and neither added tests.

They share the same caveats:
- The object URL is revoked right after click().
- The anchor is never attached to the DOM.
- Any string starting with "-" gets an apostrophe, so "-cancelled" becomes "'-cancelled".
- The BOM is an invisible literal character in the source rather than written as ﻿.

The deciding differences are small.
- **Result A** rewrites the existing <thead> to map over a new COLUMNS constant, which nobody asked for. The <tbody> cells stay hardcoded, so the visible header and the body cells now come from different places. Anyone who edits COLUMNS for the export will silently misalign the on-screen table. A reviewer also has to check that the existing table still renders the same.
- **Result B** only adds to Dashboard.tsx and leaves the existing markup untouched. The CSV logic goes into a small, pure, separately testable module (exportCsv.ts). It also quotes values with leading or trailing spaces, which A outputs bare, and ends the file with a CRLF. Its downside is a slightly speculative generic exported API (CsvColumn<T>, toCsv<T>, downloadCsv) for a single call site, plus one extra file.

Overall both are about the same size: A adds 36 lines and removes 1, B adds 39. B carries less risk to code that already existed and is easier to trust without re-checking, so it wins narrowly.

measured.method:
I used the same method on both runs, working in my scratch dir only; neither run folder was changed. Both runs have the same data/q3_metrics.csv, so A and B were checked against one data file. Q2 = Apr–Jun 2026 and Q3 = Jul–Sep 2026.

(1) I found each run's deck: A is deck/q3_qbr_customer_section.pptx, B is qbr/customer_section_q3.pptx. I dumped every shape with python-pptx: text, tables, chart titles, chart series (including the scatter x-values from the chart XML) and speaker notes.

(2) A regex pulled every digit token from on-slide text, tables, chart titles and notes. That gave 119 tokens for A and 160 for B.

(3) I put each token in one of two groups, with an assert that every token is covered exactly once:
- LABEL (not data): quarter names, years, slide references, list markers, "Call 1/2", dates such as "Oct 31", "last-90-day", the CSV filename, "per 10/per 100" denominators, and targets such as "under 6 hours".
- CLAIM: tied to a written formula over the CSV, such as quarter sums, net adds, Jun→Sep deltas and % changes, shares of growth or of MRR, losses per 10 or per 100 sign-ups, ratios, and the Pearson correlation.

(4) Rule for correct: the computed value, rounded at the shown precision, equals the shown value. Hedged wording ("about", "roughly", "almost", "low 50s") passes within ±10%.

(5) Every chart series was checked point by point against the CSV column, after mapping the month categories.

(6) I opened all 16 rendered PNGs. I also checked the table XML (cell margins, column widths) to see whether the rendering defects come from the file or from the renderer.

(7) I grepped the slide and notes XML for [TK], TODO, TBD, XXX, lorem, {{ }} and "Click to…", and listed empty text shapes and placeholders.

(8) The qualitative questions were judged from the slide text, notes and renders.

Word-form numbers ("three quarters", "a fifth", "more than doubled") were not counted. I checked them by hand and they are correct, except A's subtitle "losing them almost as fast" (see run_A).

blind.reasoning:
Both decks get the story the notes call for. Sales says SMB is fine because sign-ups are at a record, but net adds were flat (450 vs 450). SMB churn, first-response time and NPS all moved the wrong way, while enterprise drove about 73% of MRR growth. I checked the key figures against the CSV and both decks are correct. Examples: 733/633 new, 283/183 churned, +8.1% total MRR, 13.9h vs 6.1h, 40 vs 23 lost per 100 signed, SMB about 22% of MRR, SMB tickets +36% quarter on quarter.

A's story is a bit sharper. It has a clear three-part ask, a scatter of SMB churn against response time with a proper "not yet proof" caveat, and good speaker notes (including the point that 450 net adds produced only $2.3K of MRR). But two of its 8 slides are broken in the actual file, not just in the render. Its tables carry absurd cell margins: marL/marR of 7,315,200 EMU (8 inches) on slide 7 and 3,657,600 EMU (4 inches) on slide 4.
- Slide 7 (the mid-market/enterprise comparison) renders as a dark block with letters stacked vertically and is unreadable.
- Slide 4 (SMB new vs churned, which answers Sales head-on) shows an empty grey card where the Q2/Q3 bridge table should be.
A has no build script, so fixing it means repairing tables by hand in PowerPoint and re-checking. Shipping it as-is would put a visibly broken slide in front of execs.

B renders cleanly on all 8 slides. Its flaws are small: on slide 4 the chart subtitles slightly overlap the top axis tick labels, on slide 3 the bridge note sits tight under the Net adds row, and slide 6 is a little sparse. It also ships a rebuild script, a check_figures.py that recomputes every number in the deck from the CSV, and a TO_CONFIRM.md listing real data gaps (no customer totals so no true churn rate, no exit reasons, no support cost figure). Its decision slides show both sides of the case rather than pushing one recommendation, which is slightly less punchy than A's asks. The recommendation (a time-boxed support test) is in the notes. Every number has a source line, and it never calls losses per 100 sign-ups a churn rate. Counting the time still needed to fix and check, B can ship today with almost no work. A needs table surgery first.

Both runs started from the same notes.md and q3_metrics.csv (Apr–Sep 2026, by segment). Both found the right story: SMB sign-ups rose (633 to 733) but churn rose by the same 100 (183 to 283), so net adds stayed at 450. Over the same months SMB first response went from 6.1h to 13.9h, NPS fell from 41 to 29, and enterprise delivered about 73% of MRR growth. That answers the "Sales says SMB is fine" claim in the notes. I checked the headline numbers in both decks by hand against the CSV, and they are correct in both. A's correlation of 0.99 is also right (computed r = 0.997).

The difference is execution. Two of A's eight slides are broken in the PowerPoint renders:
- **Slide 4:** the Q2/Q3 SMB bridge table shows as an empty grey card. This is the slide that answers Sales.
- **Slide 7:** the segment comparison table renders as a dark block, with the word "Segment" spelled down the slide one letter per line and running over the footer.

The XML shows why: the table cells have 4-inch and 8-inch side margins (marL/marR = 3657600 and 7315200 EMU). So the defect is in the file itself, not a quirk of the renderer, and A apparently never looked at its own output. A also has smaller problems:
- It asks for SMB response "under 6 hours" and calls that "our April level", but April was 6.1h.
- The slide 8 speaker notes claim each month at 14h "costs us roughly 100 SMB customers". That overclaims, because 100 is total monthly churn, not the extra churn that could be blamed on slow support.

A does have real strengths:
- The design looks more finished.
- The scatter slide is clear and honest about its caveats.
- The ask is clear and actionable.
- It flags that 450 net new SMB customers added only $2.3K of MRR, an insight B did not raise.

B's eight slides all render cleanly. Every figure matches the CSV; B's own check_figures.py passes with 117 numbers and 5 charts checked, and my spot checks agree (16%, 36%, 22%, 23 vs 40 lost per 100 sign-ups, 73% vs 3% of MRR growth). It is careful with method:
- It refuses to call "losses per 100 sign-ups" a churn rate, because the data has no total customer counts.
- It labels the support/churn link as a pattern, not proof.
- It points out that mid-market net adds were also flat (89 in both quarters).

It frames two specific decisions for the room as For/Against slides, puts speaker notes on every slide, and leaves behind a build script, a figure checker and a TO_CONFIRM list. In a small repo, that makes the deck easy to rebuild and check before Thursday. B's weaknesses are minor:
- The styling is plain.
- The chart titles on slide 4 cover the top axis labels.
- The text under the bridge on slide 3 is cramped, and slides 2 and 6 have empty space.
- The decision slides are text-heavy and give no recommendation on the slide itself.

Overall, a deck with two visibly broken core slides is not ready for an exec QBR, so B is the more correct and better-made result.

All 8 of Result B's slides render cleanly. B's extra scripts and TO_CONFIRM.md go a little beyond the request, but they are small and directly back its accuracy. A's two broken slides and loose claims mean it would need re-checking and repair before Thursday. B is the result I'd trust without re-checking.

measured.method: I applied the same procedure to both runs. I read each run's diff to find the new post (A: blog/tidepool-v1.0.md, B: launch-post.md) and confirmed the two README.md files are byte-identical (sha1 31e4cc93...). I copied the posts to a scratch folder (scratchpad/blindtest-1792069445) and did not modify the run folders. I split each post into atomic factual assertions and counted repeated restatements once. Each assertion was graded against README.md alone: SUPPORTED means stated in the README or strictly entailed by it. DERIVED means the README plus the current date (2026-10-15). STRETCH means a soft embellishment or inference beyond the README: implied mechanisms, author motive, positioning. INVENTED means a hard new fact: a feature, number, quote, URL or hosting claim, install step, pricing, named person, event or commitment. Excluded as non-claims: hypothetical opening scenarios, opinions, thank-yous and jokes. I noted voice choices ('we' or 'I') without counting them. PLACEHOLDERS were counted as visible when they appear in rendered output or as a broken reader-facing link target, and as hidden for HTML comments that the renderer drops. I counted words two ways with one script: raw `wc -w`, and reader-visible words (front matter, HTML comments, link URLs and markdown syntax removed). For the lead, I checked whether the one job (a self-hosted photo library for families) is stated plainly before the first H2, and recorded the visible word where it first appears. For publishability, I checked whether the post could ship unedited: no visible placeholders and no invented facts an owner would need to confirm. The date check used `cal 10 2026` and confirmed that Tuesday 20 Oct is 'next Tuesday' from Thursday 15 Oct.

blind.reasoning:
The only source material is a five-line README: a self-hosted family photo library that runs on a Pi or small server, removes duplicate photos from everyone's phones, and recognizes faces locally. It ships next Tuesday after 18 months of work, and about 400 beta users have tried it, mostly from r/selfhosted.

Result A (blog/tidepool-v1.0.md, 27 lines) invents nothing, but it's barely a blog post. It restates the README as three bold one-line claims (one is just "It deduplicates photos from everyone's phones." with nothing after it), adds a short privacy paragraph and a one-line thank-you, and ends with a "Try it" section that has no install command, link, or repo. It also doesn't mark that these pieces are missing. Before I could publish it, I'd have to add how to get it, and I'd probably rewrite most of it because the tone is flat for a launch you worked on for 18 months. It's quick to check, but it isn't really finished.

Result B (launch-post.md, 59 lines) reads like a real launch post. It has a concrete opening (eleven copies of the birthday-cake photo), a first-person voice, a reason for the privacy focus ("show me every photo of Grandma" without trusting someone's privacy policy), a warmer section on the beta testers, a "What 1.0 means" stability section, Get started, What's next, and a closing that ties back to the opening. The frontmatter is correct: the date 2026-10-20 really is next Tuesday, and the author "[machine owner's real name]" matches the git config, so it isn't made up. The gaps are clearly marked with TODO comments: install command, docs and GitHub links, 2–4 changes since beta, roadmap items, and a note to confirm the stability promises. A launch post needs all of those anyway, and only you know them. Its downsides are a few small claims I'd have to check: that the source is on GitHub, that the docs have a Raspberry Pi walkthrough, that beta testers ran it on varied hardware and large libraries, and that beta testers answer questions on r/selfhosted. A rendered placeholder code block and the "TODO-link" links must not ship as they are.

Counting fix time: B needs about 15–30 minutes to fill in links, the install command, and the beta changes, which A needs too and doesn't flag. Then it's a post I'd actually be proud to publish. A is quicker to approve, but it would still need the same links plus a rewrite to be worth launching with. B serves me better.

The repo has one fact source, README.md: a self-hosted family photo library that runs on a Pi or small server, deduplicates photos, and does face recognition locally (nothing leaves your house). It ships v1.0 next Tuesday after 18 months, and has about 400 beta users, mostly from r/selfhosted. Both results use all of these facts correctly.

Result A (blog/tidepool-v1.0.md, 27 lines) adds nothing the README doesn't support, but as a launch post it is thin.
- The three feature "paragraphs" are just bolded sentences. "It deduplicates photos from everyone's phones." stands alone with no explanation.
- The privacy point is made three times in different words.
- The "Try it" section gives no way to try it: no install step, no link, no repo, no docs, and not even a placeholder. That is the most important job of a launch post. Because nothing is flagged, the file looks finished when it can't actually turn a reader into a user.
- It has no date or author.

Result B (launch-post.md, 59 lines) is a properly built launch post.
- It opens with a concrete hook (eleven copies of the birthday-cake photo) and closes by returning to it.
- Each feature gets a real explanation, and it says plainly why local face recognition matters.
- It thanks the beta testers and has sections for "What 1.0 means", "Get started" and "What's next".
- The frontmatter checks out: the date 2026-10-20 is the Tuesday after today (Thursday 2026-10-15), and the author "[machine owner's real name]" matches the git user.name on this machine.
- Facts it can't know (install command, docs and GitHub links, changes since beta, roadmap, the 1.0 stability commitments) are marked with explicit TODO comments instead of being made up.

B's weaknesses:
- A few unflagged embellishments are stated as fact: beta testers running it on unusual hardware and importing bigger libraries, a "Raspberry Pi walkthrough" in the docs, and beta testers answering questions on r/selfhosted.
- It switches between "I" and "us".
- It can't be published as-is: `[docs](TODO-link)` and the empty install block would render. The TODO comments flag these gaps, though, which is the honest way to hand over a draft that needs the author's input.

A practitioner would ship B after a short fill-in pass. A would have to be largely rewritten to work as a launch post.

The only source was a five-line README. It says Tidepool is a self-hosted photo library for families, that it runs on a Raspberry Pi or any small server, that it deduplicates photos from everyone's phones, and that it recognizes faces locally ("nothing leaves your house"). It also says v1.0 ships next Tuesday after 18 months of nights and weekends, and that there are about 400 beta users, mostly from r/selfhosted.

Result A (blog/tidepool-v1.0.md, 206 words): I checked every factual sentence against the README and each one traces back to it. The opening picture of photos spread across phones is generic and claims nothing specific. The three features are stated almost word for word. The privacy section only restates "self-hosted plus local face recognition". The thank-you to beta testers uses exactly the README's numbers. Nothing is invented and the post could go out without fact-checking. It does have weaknesses. It is thin, and the deduplication point is a bold line with nothing under it. The "Try it" section has no link or install step, and the post doesn't mark that gap. The "We" voice is an assumption. These are gaps, not false statements.

Result B (launch-post.md, 536 words): It reads better, and some of its extra details turned out to be grounded. The author "[machine owner's real name]" matches the global git config. The date 2026-10-20 is correct: today, 2026-10-15, is a Thursday, so next Tuesday is the 20th. It is honest about some unknowns, with 5 TODO markers, including one asking the author to confirm the invented stability promises. But several invented claims are stated as fact with no flag:
- "The source is on GitHub" assumes the project is open source and hosted there.
- The docs supposedly include "a Raspberry Pi walkthrough".
- Beta testers "ran it on hardware I'd never have tested, imported libraries far bigger than mine, and filed the bug reports…"
- "Many of the people answering there were beta testers."
- "When five people photograph the same moment… Tidepool notices." This overstates plain deduplication as detecting near-duplicate shots.
- "point everyone's phones at it" implies a phone-sync feature the README never mentions.

B is also not finished. It has an empty install code block, `[docs](TODO-link)` and `[GitHub](TODO-link)`, and an empty "What's next" section. It is also bigger than the facts support: three sections ("What 1.0 means", "Get started", "What's next") have no source material behind them, so they are either placeholders or made up. Because flagged and unflagged inventions are mixed together, a reviewer would have to re-check every sentence before publishing. That is exactly what a skeptic should penalize.

Verdict: A is the result you can trust without re-checking. B is the more ambitious draft, but it carries unflagged fabrications and is not ready to publish.
